01 Photovoltaic recycling

Laser processing for photovoltaic recycling

DOE-funded research · Published work

End-of-life photovoltaic modules contain valuable silver, silicon, and glass, but recovering these materials is complicated by the interfaces that hold the device together. A useful recycling process must separate the desired material while limiting damage and contamination in the remaining layers. My work develops selective laser processes that connect material recovery with process control, characterization, and automation.

Selective silver recovery

I developed complementary recovery routes for silicon and CIGS solar cells: pulsed-laser ablation in liquid to produce silver nanoparticles and microparticles, and infrared laser debonding to recover bulk silver. The central challenge was to remove the metallic contacts without unnecessarily exposing or damaging the underlying semiconductor. I established processing conditions by adjusting wavelength and pulse regime, energy input, focal position, scan speed, overlap, pass count, and the surrounding medium.

I used SEM to assess the size and morphology of the recovered silver, EDS to examine composition and purity, and UV-Vis spectroscopy to characterize nanoparticle optical response. Microscopy, spectroscopy, and electrical measurements of the processed cells connected recovery conditions to changes in the remaining device structure. These studies demonstrated distinct routes to particulate and bulk silver recovery, with the processing strategy selected around the desired product and substrate response.

Backsheet removal and PV delamination

Recovering the other module components requires controlled separation of the laminated stack. I developed a through-glass laser process that deposits heat at the silicon-EVA interface, weakening adhesion to enable separation of the EVA and PVDF-PET backsheet structure while preserving the glass and silicon wafer. By varying laser power, scan conditions, and processing time, I mapped the transition between useful delamination and unwanted polymer softening, bubbling, or carbonization.

I developed transient thermal models of the multilayer glass/Si/EVA structure to relate temperature evolution to the observed separation behavior. Raman, FTIR, optical microscopy, profilometry, and electrical measurements provided complementary checks on the recovered materials. The resulting process demonstrated backsheet removal and interfacial delamination while retaining the glass and silicon, extending the recycling workflow beyond metal recovery.

Automation and upscaling

Moving toward higher throughput requires a process that can accommodate irregular fragments and varying electrode patterns. I developed a U-Net/OpenCV workflow to identify silver contacts, extract their geometry, translate coordinates, and generate vector scan paths for Galil stages and galvo execution. Selective scanning directs the laser to the target features and reduces unnecessary exposure of neighboring material. The electrode-detection task achieved greater than 98% pixel-level segmentation accuracy.

I also integrated LIBS-based process monitoring into the broader recovery workflow and evaluated processing conditions with recovery yield, purity, throughput, and energy use in mind. Together, the published silver-recovery and delamination studies establish a foundation for upscaling through automated targeting, controlled energy delivery, and material-specific validation. The segmentation accuracy describes feature detection; it is distinct from recovery yield and positioning accuracy.

02 Multimodal spectroscopy

Multimodal Raman, fluorescence, LIBS spectroscopy and imaging

NASA-funded research · Manuscript under review

A planetary material can reveal different information through its molecular vibrations, optical emission, elemental composition, and surface features. Combining Raman, fluorescence, laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS), and imaging makes it possible to relate these complementary observations to the same sample region. I built a custom instrument from the optical layout through integration and characterization to provide that measurement capability on a shared platform.

One laser, complementary measurements

The key design choice was a single 355 nm nanosecond pulsed laser. With suitable excitation and collection conditions, it provides the energy for ablation and plasma emission in LIBS, excites fluorescence, and generates Raman scattering. Sharing the source and optical paths allows the measurement modes to interrogate a common region, making their results easier to compare and interpret.

I developed the optical layout and integrated shared excitation and collection optics, reflective optics, spectral filters, fiber-coupled spectrometry, imaging, and motorized XYZ sample positioning. I assembled and aligned the components, established the signal paths, and coordinated focusing and sample positioning across the spectroscopic and imaging modes.

Building the instrument required resolving coupled optical and mechanical issues. I debugged signal loss and background contributions, adjusted spectral filtering and collection geometry, and checked alignment drift and positioning repeatability. Keeping the measurements co-located required attention to both optical focus and stage motion, so I tested repeatability across modes as part of the integration process.

I used the completed platform to characterize planetary materials and interpret complementary spectroscopic signatures from the same sample region. The instrument brought Raman, fluorescence, LIBS, and imaging into one custom measurement workflow, with structural and electrical/material characterization providing additional context for relating the signals to material properties.

The manuscript on this planetary-materials spectroscopy platform is under review in the IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Quantum Electronics.

03 Crystal growth and materials

Single-crystal growth, thin films, and functional materials

IIT Delhi · Published collaborative research

Reliable measurements of electronic and energy materials begin with controlled sample preparation. At IIT Delhi, I worked across single-crystal growth, pulsed laser deposition, and high-vacuum processing to connect fabrication conditions with material structure and functional response.

I grew and processed chalcogenide materials including Sb₂Te₃ and MnSb₂Te₄, operated and troubleshot vacuum and deposition equipment, and developed repeatable sample-preparation workflows. This work required control of the processing environment and careful evaluation of the material produced at each stage.

I combined SEM/TEM, XRD, XPS, PPMS, and electrical/electrochemical measurements to examine morphology, crystal structure, composition, and physical behavior. Comparing complementary measurements helped relate changes in preparation conditions to the observed properties rather than relying on a single characterization method.

I also contributed as a co-author to a published investigation of MoSeTe as an anode for sodium-ion batteries. The study connected structural characterization with electrochemical performance, extending this process-property approach to materials for energy storage.

04 Transparent conducting oxides

Transparent conducting oxide thin films

IIT Ropar · Published work

Transparent electrodes must transmit light while conducting electrical current. Achieving both properties depends on the interaction between deposition conditions, oxidation, and the resulting film structure. My MSc research at IIT Ropar investigated this relationship in antimony-doped tin oxide films.

I fabricated metallic precursor layers by vacuum thermal evaporation and converted them into Sb-doped SnO₂ through controlled post-oxidation. I varied precursor thickness and processing conditions to examine how the coupled deposition and oxidation steps influenced the final film.

I characterized crystal structure with XRD, measured optical transmission, and evaluated film thickness and electrical resistivity. Assessing these properties together allowed me to compare processing conditions in terms of both optical and electrical behavior.

The resulting first-author study on 5 wt% Sb-doped SnO₂, published in AIP Conference Proceedings, connected fabrication and post-treatment with film structure, transparency, and resistivity.

05 Low-light imaging

Low-light imaging and statistical noise analysis

Ongoing research

At low light levels, sensor noise can obscure the features an image is meant to measure. Evaluating image restoration therefore requires understanding the recorded signal and its uncertainty, as well as the visual appearance of the output.

I work with RAW image data, statistical noise models, and Python-based analysis to examine how noise affects image formation and restoration. Working from the underlying measurements allows me to investigate signal and noise behavior before display processing changes the image.

I use controlled comparisons to evaluate restoration results and distinguish improved visual appearance from preservation of the measured information. This ongoing work develops an analysis framework for interpreting low-signal images and assessing the reliability of recovered features.

06 TEM and cathodoluminescence

Electron microscopy and cathodoluminescence of photovoltaic contacts

Manuscript in preparation

Microscopy shows where structural features occur, while cathodoluminescence probes the light emitted when a material is excited by electrons. Examining the two together can help relate local structure to optical response in photovoltaic contact stacks.

I analyze electron microscopy images and cathodoluminescence measurements of TiOₓ/Al₂O₃/Si contacts. My work focuses on interpreting spectral features alongside the material structure and determining which observations remain consistent through the analysis workflow.

I test spectral reconstruction and interference corrections to distinguish repeatable material signals from processing artifacts. This work is ongoing, with a manuscript in preparation; the analysis is directed toward a more reliable interpretation of local optical response in these multilayer contacts.
